Twenty-six comments

Now here’s something you don’t see every day: a reel in the key of F and a fine reel it is.

If you’re really uncomfortable with playing this tune in F you could transpose it up to G, but then you’re going to have to stretch as far as the high C note.

The F note that opens the tune and recurs in the first part can be played as a roll or as triplet (FGF or FAF).

↳ Posted by Jeremy on June 1st, 2001.

Hooray for Brother Steve, who identified this tune in a set by the Bradley Bros. for me. Liam and Anthony play this set as follows:

Beare Island Reel (2x)
Humors of Westport (2x, B first, then A)
Seany Dorris (3x)
Humors of Westport (1 B and 1 A)

A really mighty set, and a helluva lot of fun to play (and to dance to!).

Their setting of this tune is very similar to Jeremy’s, as in:

Re: The Humours Of Westport

There must be an interesting explanation for why this tune is in F. Here’s my hypothesis:
On a summer evening, a bunch of blue-grassers are playing music at some brewery. The lead guitarist whimsically says, “You know what, lets play this tune in F!” The banjo player approves, puts a million cabos on his banjo, and says, “Lets hit dem new notes!” Chaos ensues.

Re: The Humours Of Westport

“The Humours Of Westport” is in “O’Neill’s 1001” - #457 [ my edotion ] - key of “F”.
According to “Wikipedia” : “Bluegrass music is a form of American roots music named after Kentucky mandolin player and songwriter Bill Monroe’s band, the Bluegrass Boys [2] 1939-96, ….. ”
“The Humours Of Westport” in “F” precedes “Bluegrass” by at least 32 years.
QED.

McBand’s

Simple transcription with no variations or ornamentation.

I see this tune It is in Selected Tunes from
“Johnny O’Leary of Sliabh Luachra”
(ed. Terry Moylan; Dublin 1994). That’s where I took the name from.

But this setting of the tune is not like the one in the book. This one is another setting I first heard from the Breton band Gwendal in their album Rainy Day, first track. They play this reel from 4:13 to 5:12 here (I added a comment with the link that will get you directly to the beginning):

https://youtu.be/nQvj5NmOFZA

They happen to play the parts the other way around as it is in the book of Johnny O’Leary’s tunes. I have kept the same order in the parts as in the book.

Pat Barton also plays this setting of the tune in one of the videos in his YouTube channel. He plays the parts in the same order as in the book. He gives the tune another name: Because He Was A Bonny Lad.

↳ Posted by Fernando Durbán Galnares on December 4th, 2020.

Re: The Humours Of Westport

I have a very basic question: on fiddle or mandolin, when rocking back and forth between the f on the D string, do people normally rock on the index finger or the middle finger? As a beginner, I want to be a good boy and cover the right part of the neck with the correct fingers but it feels horrible using the middle finger currently. Happy to suck it up and learn it but not if nobody else bothers to do so.

↳ Posted by Lye_Valley_Ned on May 10th, 2021.

Re: The Humours Of Westport

It would be your middle finger on the F# on the D string, Lye_Valley_Ned. Otherwise you’d come unstuck when you got to the B note (normally index finger) at the start of the fourth bar.
Playing the F# with your index finger would put you in 2nd position, which is very rarely used in trad playing.

↳ Posted by DonaldK on May 10th, 2021.

Re: The Humours Of Westport

The Humours Of Westport, X:8

This is the lovely version played by John Carty and Michael McGoldrick on the CD ‘At our Leisure’. The tune rolls along effortlessly with their playing. Curiously on the recording the first part is repeated (as written here) on the first time through the tune only, thereafter the second part is played as written here for the repeat. McGoldrick is playing the tune on a ‘C’ chanter.
